---
title: "Week 1: Tools of Reproducible Work"
subtitle: "From your laptop to an automatically checked public repository"
---

## Goal for today

After this class, you will be able to:

- edit and run a Python notebook in Visual Studio Code,
- record your changes with Git,
- push your commits to GitHub, and
- check the automatic test result on GitHub Actions.

## What Visual Studio Code does

Visual Studio Code is a **code editor**: one window where you write code, run it, see the results, and record your changes. In this course you use it to:

- write Python files (`.py`) and notebooks (`.ipynb`),
- run them and see the output,
- type commands in its built-in terminal,
- see what changed in your files and send those changes to GitHub.

Visual Studio Code does not run Python by itself. It hands your code to the Python in your course environment. The name in the bottom-right corner (for a `.py` file) or the top-right corner (for a notebook) tells you which Python that is.

### Python file versus notebook

| | Python file | Jupyter notebook |
|---|---|---|
| Extension | `.py` | `.ipynb` |
| Runs | The whole file, top to bottom | One cell at a time, in any order |
| Stores | Code only | Code, text, math, plots, and outputs |
| Good for | Running a whole analysis the same way, start to finish | Running a few lines at a time and seeing each result right away |

: {tbl-colwidths="[16,42,42]"}

That freedom is also the risk: because cells can run in any order, always check a finished notebook by **Restart Kernel → Run All**.

### Git versus GitHub

| Git | GitHub |
|---|---|
| Software on your computer | A website that hosts repositories |
| Records the history of your changes (`add`, `commit`) | Stores pushed commits, shares them, and runs automatic checks |
| Works offline | Needs the internet |

Think of Git as keeping a **recipe notebook** while you develop a chocolate chip cookie recipe:

- **Working directory**: your kitchen. You try things out here: more sugar, maybe coconut chips. Every edit you save lands here first.
- **Staging area**: the counter. `git add week1.ipynb` sets out what you have decided to include in this version of the recipe. Nothing is written down yet, and you can still put things back.
- **Local history**: your recipe notebook. `git commit` writes down everything on the counter as a new version, with a note such as "less sugar, no coconut". Earlier versions stay in the notebook, so you can always go back to one.
- **GitHub**: your recipe blog. `git push` posts the versions in your notebook. Only written-down versions can be posted, never what is still on the counter.

So the order is always: edit and save → `git add` → `git commit` → `git push`.

## Lab 1 — Planted bugs

1. Open the [`week1-starter`](https://github.com/yoonismo/week1-starter) repository on GitHub and click **Use this template** → **Create a new repository**. Create it in *your* account and name it `week1`.
2. On *your* new repository, click the green **Code** button and copy the HTTPS address. For a student whose GitHub username is `jdoe`, it is `https://github.com/jdoe/week1.git`.
3. In the Terminal, move into your course folder:

    ```bash
    cd ~/ECON481
    ```

    Windows:

    ```powershell
    cd ~\ECON481
    ```

4. Clone your copy (use **your own** address):

    ```bash
    git clone https://github.com/jdoe/week1.git
    ```

5. In Visual Studio Code, choose **File → Open Folder…** and open the new `week1` folder (the folder, not just one file).
6. Open `week1.ipynb`. Click **Select Kernel** → **Jupyter Kernel…** → **ECON 481 (Python 3.12)**.
7. Run the cells in order and answer the questions in the notebook:
    - **Question 1.** At what values of $x$ does $2x = x^2$? Solve it **by hand**.
    - **Question 2.** If two functions agree at some values, are they the same function?
    - **Question 3.** Ask an LLM how to write "$x$ squared" in Python. Ask it to **explain, not to rewrite** the notebook.
    - **Question 4.** The check cell passes. Is that good news?

    The last section of the notebook, *lists versus arrays*, is optional. 

## Lab 2 — Fix, commit, push

1. In `week1.ipynb`, scroll to the section **2. Check**. Below **Question 4** there is a code cell:

    ```python
    assert squared(2) == 4
    print("Check passed")
    ```

    This cell tests the function at a single point. In that same cell, replace the first line, `assert squared(2) == 4`, with a check at all 61 points of `grid` (the grid you plotted on):

    ```python
    assert np.allclose(squared(grid), grid ** 2)
    ```

    Run the cell. It fails with an `AssertionError` — good. That is the bug being caught.

2. Fix `squared`. Then **Restart Kernel → Run All**.
3. **Clear All Outputs**, then save the notebook (**⌘ S**; Windows: **Ctrl + S**).
4. In the Terminal, move into your repository:

    ```bash
    cd ~/ECON481/week1
    ```

    Windows:

    ```powershell
    cd ~\ECON481\week1
    ```

5. See what changed:

    ```bash
    git status
    ```

6. Choose the file to record:

    ```bash
    git add week1.ipynb
    ```

7. Record it with a message:

    ```bash
    git commit -m "Fix squared() and strengthen the check"
    ```

8. Send it to GitHub:

    ```bash
    git push
    ```

9. On GitHub, open the **Actions** tab and watch the workflow run.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Lesson
An automatic check catches only what you ask it to check. The one-point check would have passed with the bug still in place.
:::

## Lab 3 — A deliberate red X

In this lab you make the GitHub check fail on purpose, read why, and fix it. You work in the same `week1` repository as in Lab 2.

1. Next week we use `pandas`. Install it **only on your own machine**, into the course environment. First, activate the course environment (this works from any folder):

    ```bash
    source ~/ECON481/.venv/bin/activate
    ```

    Windows:

    ```powershell
    ~\ECON481\.venv\Scripts\activate
    ```

    Then install pandas:

    ```bash
    uv pip install pandas
    ```

2. In Visual Studio Code, open `week1.ipynb`. In the first code cell (under **0. Setup**), add one new line below `import numpy as np`:

    ```python
    import pandas as pd
    ```

    Run the cell. It works on your laptop, because pandas is now in your course environment.

3. **Clear All Outputs** and save the notebook. Then, in the Terminal, move into your repository:

    ```bash
    cd ~/ECON481/week1
    ```

    Windows:

    ```powershell
    cd ~\ECON481\week1
    ```

    Record and send the change:

    ```bash
    git add week1.ipynb
    ```

    ```bash
    git commit -m "Import pandas"
    ```

    ```bash
    git push
    ```

4. On GitHub, open the **Actions** tab. This time the run **fails** with a red X.
5. Click the failed run, then the job **run-notebook**, then the step **Run the notebook from top to bottom**. Near the end of the log you will find:

    ```
    ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pandas'
    ```

    Ask an LLM to explain this error — **without** changing any files.

    The reason: GitHub's machine does not have your laptop's environment. It installs only the packages listed in `requirements.txt`, and pandas is not on that list.

6. In Visual Studio Code, open `requirements.txt` (in the `week1` folder, next to `week1.ipynb`). It lists one package per line. Add a new line at the end:

    ```
    pandas
    ```

    Save the file.

7. Record and send this change too (you are still inside `week1`):

    ```bash
    git add requirements.txt
    ```

    ```bash
    git commit -m "Add pandas to requirements.txt"
    ```

    ```bash
    git push
    ```

8. Open the **Actions** tab again and watch the new run turn green.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Lesson
"It works on my computer" is not reproducibility. Reproducibility starts with *declaring* your dependencies.
:::

## Lab 4 — Pull

1. On the GitHub website, edit `README.md` (add your name) and commit it there.
2. On your laptop, inside your repository, bring that change down:

    ```bash
    git pull
    ```

3. Check that `README.md` now shows your name.

When other people may also change the repository, remember the order:

> **pull → edit → save → add → commit → push**

## What a green check means

A green check means that every command in the workflow finished without error, for that commit, on a fresh machine.

It does **not** mean that

- the causal assumptions hold,
- the research design is valid,
- the estimates are correct, or
- the code is free of logical errors.

Its value depends entirely on what you told it to check.

## Rules for using LLMs in this course

1. Never paste passwords, access tokens, private data, or personal information.
2. Ask for an explanation before you ask for a change.
3. You run every command and make every edit yourself — and you check the result.

:::
